title: Convert Date Format
statement:
One table holds a list of calendar dates:

- `Days(day)`: one row per date; `day` is a `DATE` and is unique.

Rewrite every date as text of the form `"<weekday>, <month> <day>, <year>"`, for example `2022-04-12` becomes `Tuesday, April 12, 2022`:

- the weekday and the month are written out in full in English, starting with a capital letter;
- the day of the month has **no leading zero** (`August 9`, not `August 09`);
- the year has four digits.

Return one row per date with a single column named `day` holding the text. Rows may come in any order.
constraints: Every day is a valid date written as YYYY-MM-DD
brute:
SELECT CONCAT(DAYNAME(d.day), ', ', MONTHNAME(d.day), ' ', DAYOFMONTH(d.day), ', ', YEAR(d.day)) AS day
FROM Days AS d
notes:
## Intuition

This is pure formatting: each date maps to one string and no row depends on another. MySQL's `DATE_FORMAT(date, pattern)` builds the string from a pattern in which `%` codes stand for parts of the date and every other character is copied as it is. The whole task is choosing the right codes.

## Approach

1. Read every row of `Days`.
2. Format it with the pattern `'%W, %M %e, %Y'`:
   - `%W` is the full weekday name (`Tuesday`);
   - `%M` is the full month name (`April`);
   - `%e` is the day of the month **without** a leading zero (`9`), unlike `%d` (`09`);
   - `%Y` is the four-digit year;
   - the comma after the weekday, the spaces and the comma before the year are literal text.
3. Name the result column `day`, the same name as the input column.

## Example 1, step by step

- `2022-04-12`: `%W` = Tuesday, `%M` = April, `%e` = 12, `%Y` = 2022, giving `Tuesday, April 12, 2022`.
- `2021-08-09`: Monday, August, `%e` drops the zero of `09`, giving `Monday, August 9, 2021`.
- `2020-06-26`: `Friday, June 26, 2020`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(N) for N dates; each is formatted once.
- Space: O(N) for the result.

## Pitfalls

- `%d` keeps the leading zero (`August 09`), and `%D` adds an English suffix (`9th`); only `%e` gives `9` (Test 7).
- `%a` and `%b` are the three-letter abbreviations (`Tue`, `Apr`); the output needs full names.
- `%y` is a two-digit year, and `%m` is the month number, not its name.
- Building the text with `CONCAT` also works, but then every separator (`', '`, `' '`) must be typed by hand and in the right place.

## Clauses

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `DATE_FORMAT(day, ...)` | turns the date into text following the pattern |
| `'%W, %M %e, %Y'` | weekday, comma, month, day without zero, comma, year |
| `day` (output) | the formatted text, under the input column's name |

narration.1: One output column per row of Days; no joins or grouping are needed.
narration.2: DATE_FORMAT turns a date into text by following a pattern.
narration.3: The value to format is the row's date.
narration.4: Full weekday, comma, full month, day of month without a leading zero, comma, four-digit year.
narration.5: The formatted text is returned under the column name day.
narration.6: Every row of Days is converted; nothing is filtered out.
